title: Registry of Gospels and Their Canonical Status
html:
Registry of Gospels and Their Canonical Status

This registry lists every gospel and gospel-type text about Jesus that survives in full, survives in fragments, or is known only from ancient citations. For each one it records how the text was judged in ancient canon lists and what its canonical status is in Christian traditions today. Where this repository holds a public-domain text, the Text here column links to it.

Dates of composition are scholarly ranges. Manuscript dates are a separate thing, and many texts survive only in copies made centuries after they were written (see the dossier's distinction between event chronology and document chronology).

Status key

Status Meaning
Canonical (universal) Accepted as scripture by every Christian church today.
Canonical (historical/local) Functioned as scripture in some churches for a period but is canonical nowhere today.
Canonical (non-Christian canon) Scripture in a religion other than mainstream Christianity, e.g. Manichaeism.
Disputed (antilegomena) Read in some churches, but ancient lists placed it among disputed or spurious books. It never became canonical.
Non-canonical, liturgically influential Never scripture, but its stories shaped feasts, iconography, or saints' names in Catholic and Orthodox practice.
Rejected Named and rejected, or classed as heretical, by an ancient authority or list.
Non-canonical (unlisted) Never canonical, and absent from the ancient canon lists, often because it was lost until modern discovery.
Hypothetical / disputed authenticity A modern scholarly reconstruction, or a text whose ancient origin is contested.

Ancient authorities cited

Abbrev. Source Date
Iren. Irenaeus, Against Heresies (four-gospel argument at 3.11.8) c. 180
Orig. Origen, Homily 1 on Luke, which names the gospels of the Egyptians, the Twelve, Basilides, Thomas, and Matthias as gospels the church does not accept c. 233
Eus. Eusebius, Church History 3.25. Categories: homologoumena (accepted), antilegomena (disputed), notha (spurious), heretical c. 325
Ath. Athanasius, 39th Festal Letter: the first list of exactly the 27 NT books 367
Gel. Decretum Gelasianum, a list of rejected books (attributed to Pope Gelasius, probably 6th c.) 6th c.
Niceph. Stichometry of Nicephorus, which divides books into canonical, antilegomena, and apocrypha 9th c.

1. The canonical gospels

All four are Canonical (universal): Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox (Coptic, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Armenian, Syriac), Assyrian Church of the East, and Protestant. Iren. defends exactly four. Eus. lists them first among the homologoumena. Ath. lists them.

Gospel Composed (est.) Earliest manuscript witnesses Notes Text here
Matthew c. 80–90 P104 (2nd c.), P64+67 (c. 200) Traditionally attributed to the apostle Matthew; the work itself is anonymous. 01-matthew.md
Mark c. 66–75 P45 (3rd c.) Usually considered the earliest gospel. The longer ending (16:9–20) is absent from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus. It is canonical for Catholics (Trent) and Orthodox, and bracketed in many Protestant translations. 02-mark.md
Luke c. 80–95 P75 (c. 175–225), P4 First volume of Luke–Acts. Marcion's gospel (below) was a shorter form of it. 03-luke.md
John c. 90–110 P52 (2nd c.), P66, P75 The story of the woman taken in adultery (7:53–8:11) is absent from the earliest manuscripts. 04-john.md

2. Gospel harmonies

Gospel Composed Witnesses Ancient verdict Status today Text here
Diatessaron (Tatian) c. 170 Original (Syriac or Greek) lost. Witnesses include Ephrem's Syriac commentary (4th c.), the Arabic harmony, Codex Fuldensis (Latin, 546), and possibly the Dura-Europos fragment (before 256) The standard gospel text of Syriac-speaking churches into the 5th c. Theodoret of Cyrrhus removed some 200 copies from his diocese, and Rabbula of Edessa ordered the separate gospels to be used Canonical (historical/local): Syriac churches until the 5th c. Not canonical anywhere today. diatessaron-tatian-hogg-1896.txt

3. Sayings gospels and sayings collections

Gospel Composed Witnesses Ancient verdict Status today Text here
Gospel of Thomas c. 50–140 (disputed) Greek P.Oxy. 1, 654, 655 (c. 200–250); complete Coptic text in Nag Hammadi Codex II,2 (c. 350) Hippolytus quotes it. Orig. rejects. Eus. lists it among heretical works. Cyril of Jerusalem attributes it to Manichaeans. Niceph. apocrypha Rejected gospel-of-thomas.md (Mattison); GG 01 (Lambdin)
Q (sayings source) c. 40–70 (if it existed) No manuscript. Reconstructed from the non-Markan material shared by Matthew and Luke Unknown in antiquity Hypothetical: a modern scholarly reconstruction q-sayings-source.md
Sayings of Jesus (P.Oxy. 5575) Copy dated c. 150–200 A single Greek papyrus leaf, published in 2023 (Oxyrhynchus Papyri 87) Unknown in antiquity. Its sayings parallel Matthew, Luke, and Thomas Non-canonical (unlisted) sayings-of-jesus-p-oxy-5575.md

4. Gnostic and revelation gospels (the "Gnostic Bible")

These texts present Jesus revealing secret knowledge (gnosis), usually after the resurrection. Most come from the Nag Hammadi codices (found 1945), the Berlin Codex (BG 8502), the Askew and Bruce codices, or Codex Tchacos.

Our Gnostic Bible. The reference editions are the eleven PDFs in 0xSero/gnostic-gospels, cited below as GG 00–11. That repo's MANIFEST.json records each PDF's translator, source URL, and SHA-256. Nine of its translations are under copyright (Robinson's Nag Hammadi Library translators), so they are linked here rather than copied. Only Mattison's Mary and Judas are public domain. GG 07–09 are not gospels; they are listed at the end of this section because they belong to that set.

Gospel Composed Witnesses Ancient verdict Status today Text here
Gospel of Mary 2nd c. Greek P.Ryl. 463 and P.Oxy. 3525 (3rd c.); Coptic Berlin Codex 8502 (5th c.) Not mentioned in any ancient list Non-canonical (unlisted) gospel-of-mary.md; GG 02 (both Mattison)
Gospel of Judas c. 130–170 Codex Tchacos 3 (Coptic, radiocarbon c. 280 ± 60) Iren. 1.31.1 names it as used by the "Cainites" Rejected gospel-of-judas.md; GG 06 (both Mattison)
Gospel of Philip 2nd–3rd c. Nag Hammadi Codex II,3 (c. 350) Epiphanius quotes a "Gospel of Philip" (possibly a different work) Non-canonical (unlisted) gospel-of-philip.md (Mattison); GG 05 (Isenberg)
Gospel of Truth c. 140–180 (Valentinian) Nag Hammadi Codices I,3 and XII,2 Iren. 3.11.9 says the Valentinians had a "Gospel of Truth" Rejected gospel-of-truth.md (Mattison); GG 03 (Attridge & MacRae)
Secret Book (Apocryphon) of James 2nd c. Nag Hammadi Codex I,2 Not mentioned in any ancient list Non-canonical (unlisted) secret-book-of-james.md
The Stranger's Book (Allogenes, CT 4) 2nd–3rd c. Codex Tchacos 4 Not mentioned in any ancient list Non-canonical (unlisted) strangers-book.md
Pistis Sophia 3rd c. Askew Codex (Coptic, 4th c.?) Not mentioned in any ancient list Non-canonical (unlisted) pistis-sophia-horner-1924.txt
Untitled Text of the Bruce Codex 3rd c. Bruce Codex (Coptic) Not mentioned in any ancient list Non-canonical (unlisted) gnosis-of-the-light-lamplugh-1918.txt
Hymn and vision of the cross (Acts of John 94–102) 2nd–3rd c. Greek Acts of John manuscripts Acts of John: Eus. heretical. Rejected at the Second Council of Nicaea (787) Rejected gnostic-crucifixion-mead-1907.txt
Secret Book (Apocryphon) of John 2nd c. Nag Hammadi Codices II,1, III,1, IV,1; Berlin Codex 8502,2 Iren. 1.29 summarizes closely parallel teaching Non-canonical (unlisted) GG 04 (Waldstein & Wisse, long recension)
Gospel of the Egyptians (Coptic; Holy Book of the Great Invisible Spirit) 2nd–3rd c. (Sethian) Nag Hammadi Codices III,2 and IV,2 Not mentioned in any ancient list (distinct from the Greek work below) Non-canonical (unlisted) GG 11 (Böhlig & Wisse)
Dialogue of the Savior 2nd c. Nag Hammadi Codex III,5 Not mentioned in any ancient list Non-canonical (unlisted) GG 10 (Emmel)
Books of Jeu 3rd c. Bruce Codex Not mentioned in any ancient list Non-canonical (unlisted) —
Gospel of Eve 2nd–4th c. Lost; quoted by Epiphanius (Panarion 26) Rejected as heretical Rejected —
Gospel of Basilides 2nd c. Lost Orig. rejects Rejected —
Gospel of Matthias / Traditions of Matthias 2nd c. Lost; quoted by Clement of Alexandria Orig. and Eus. heretical. Gel. rejects Rejected —
Living Gospel of Mani 3rd c. Fragments (e.g. Cologne Mani Codex) Scripture of Manichaeism Canonical (non-Christian canon): Manichaean —
Hypostasis of the Archons (not a gospel) 3rd c. Nag Hammadi Codex II,4 Not mentioned in any ancient list Non-canonical (unlisted) GG 07 (Layton)
On the Origin of the World (not a gospel) 3rd–4th c. Nag Hammadi Codices II,5 and XIII,2 Not mentioned in any ancient list Non-canonical (unlisted) GG 08 (Bethge & Layton)
Thunder, Perfect Mind (revelation poem, not a gospel) 2nd–3rd c. Nag Hammadi Codex VI,2 Not mentioned in any ancient list Non-canonical (unlisted) GG 09 (MacRae)

5. Jewish-Christian gospels

Gospel Composed Witnesses Ancient verdict Status today Text here
Gospel of the Hebrews early–mid 2nd c. Lost; quoted by Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Jerome Eus.: "some" place it among the spurious (notha) books. Niceph.: antilegomena Disputed (antilegomena) —
Gospel of the Nazarenes 2nd c. Lost; Jerome and later marginal notes (the grouping is modern) Never accepted Non-canonical (unlisted) —
Gospel of the Ebionites 2nd c. Lost; quoted by Epiphanius (Panarion 30) Treated as heretical Rejected —

Fragments and other gospels

These are separate from the Coptic Sethian Gospel of the Egyptians in section 4 (NHC III,2 / IV,2), which is a different work despite the similar name.

Text Composed Witnesses Ancient verdict Status today Text here
Gospel of the Egyptians (Greek) 2nd c. Lost; quoted by Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 3.6, 3.9) Orig. rejects it. NASSCAL records its use by Naassenes and Sabellians, not by Jewish-Christian groups Rejected —
Gospel of the Twelve 2nd c. Lost; named by Origen and by Ambrose's prologue to Luke Orig. rejects Rejected —
Gospel of Cerinthus early 2nd c. Lost; described by Epiphanius Treated as heretical Rejected —
Gospel of Apelles 2nd c. Lost; known through Ambrose and Jerome Treated as heretical Rejected —

6. Narrative and Passion gospels

Gospel Composed Witnesses Ancient verdict Status today Text here
Gospel of Peter 2nd c. Akhmim fragment (8th–9th c. manuscript); P.Oxy. 2949 (debated) Serapion of Antioch (c. 200) first allowed it at Rhossus, then rejected it. Eus. heretical. Gel. rejects Rejected gospel-of-peter.md
Egerton Gospel (Unknown Gospel) 2nd c. P.Egerton 2 and P.Köln 255 (copy c. 150–200) Not mentioned in any ancient list Non-canonical (unlisted) egerton-gospel.md
Gospel of Nicodemus (Acts of Pilate and Descent into Hell) 4th–5th c. in its current form Greek, Latin, Coptic, Syriac, Armenian Very widely read in the medieval West. Source of the Harrowing of Hell tradition Non-canonical, liturgically influential ANF 8; Hone
Pilate cycle (Letter and Report of Pilate, Giving Up of Pilate, Death of Pilate, Narrative of Joseph of Arimathaea, Avenging of the Saviour) 4th–8th c. Greek and Latin Never canonical. The Ethiopian church venerates Pilate and his wife Procla as saints; Eastern Orthodoxy venerates Procla Non-canonical ANF 8
Secret Gospel of Mark Disputed Known only from a letter attributed to Clement of Alexandria, which Morton Smith reported finding at Mar Saba in 1958. Only photographs survive Unknown in antiquity Disputed authenticity: some scholars regard it as a modern forgery secret-gospel-of-mark.md
Gospel of Marcion c. 140 Lost; reconstructed from Tertullian and Epiphanius The sole gospel of Marcion's church. Rejected by Irenaeus, Tertullian, and others Canonical (historical/local): Marcionite church only. Rejected by proto-orthodox writers —
Gospel of Bartholomew / Questions of Bartholomew 3rd–6th c. Greek, Latin, Slavonic, Coptic Gel. rejects "Gospels in the name of Bartholomew" Rejected —
Gospel of the Savior (Unknown Berlin Gospel) 2nd–3rd c. P.Berol. 22220 (Coptic) Not mentioned in any ancient list Non-canonical (unlisted) —
Gospel of Gamaliel 5th–6th c. Coptic fragments; Ethiopic Lament of Mary Never canonical Non-canonical —
Gospel of Barnabas (medieval) 14th–16th c. Italian and Spanish manuscripts (16th c.) Unrelated to the lost "Gospel of Barnabas" rejected by Gel. Presents an Islamic portrait of Jesus Non-canonical in any church —

7. Infancy gospels

Gospel Composed Witnesses Ancient verdict Status today Text here
Infancy Gospel of James (Protevangelium) c. 150 Papyrus Bodmer V (3rd–4th c.); more than 140 Greek manuscripts Gel. rejects the "Gospel of James the Younger". Source of the names Joachim and Anne and of the feast of the Presentation of Mary Non-canonical, liturgically influential (Orthodox and Catholic) Mattison; ANF 8; Hone
Infancy Gospel of Thomas 2nd c. Earliest complete Greek manuscript: Hagios Saba 259 (11th c.); older Syriac and Latin versions Iren. 1.20.1 cites a story from it as used by the Marcosians. Gel. rejects a book "of the infancy of the Saviour" Rejected Mattison; ANF 8; Hone
Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew 7th c. (Latin) Latin manuscripts Shaped medieval Western art (e.g. the ox and ass at the manger) Non-canonical, liturgically influential ANF 8
Gospel of the Nativity of Mary 9th c. (Latin) Latin manuscripts Never canonical Non-canonical ANF 8; Hone
Arabic Infancy Gospel 5th–6th c. (Syriac origin) Arabic and Syriac Never canonical Non-canonical ANF 8; Hone
History of Joseph the Carpenter 5th–7th c. Coptic and Arabic Never canonical Non-canonical ANF 8
Armenian Infancy Gospel 6th c. or later Armenian Never canonical Non-canonical —

New Testament canon by tradition

The four gospels are canonical everywhere. Traditions differ only on the rest of the New Testament:

Tradition NT books Differences from the 27-book canon
Catholic 27 Defined dogmatically at Trent (1546).
Eastern Orthodox 27 Revelation is canonical but is not read in the liturgy.
Protestant 27 Luther questioned Hebrews, James, Jude, and Revelation and placed them last in his 1522 New Testament. They were never removed.
Coptic, Armenian, Syriac Orthodox 27 The Syriac Peshitta originally had 22 books. The other five came in through later Syriac versions (Philoxenian, Harklean). The Armenian church at times included 3 Corinthians.
Assyrian Church of the East 22 The Peshitta canon: it omits 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude, and Revelation.
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo 27 (narrower) / 35 (broader) The broader canon adds the Sinodos (4 parts), the Book of the Covenant (2), Ethiopic Clement (1), and the Ethiopic Didascalia (1). None of these is a gospel.

The full 27-book text is in collections/scripture/new-testament.

Sources for this registry

  • Eusebius, Church History 3.25; Athanasius, Festal Letter 39; Irenaeus, Against Heresies; Origen, Homily 1 on Luke. Translations: New Advent / CCEL.
  • Bart D. Ehrman and Zlatko Pleše, The Apocryphal Gospels: Texts and Translations (Oxford, 2011).
  • Bruce M. Metzger, The Canon of the New Testament (Oxford, 1987).
  • NASSCAL e-Clavis: Christian Apocrypha, which has per-text manuscript and bibliography entries.
  • Gospels.net, Mark M. Mattison's public-domain translations and manuscript notes.
  • Early Christian Writings, an index of texts, translations, and dating ranges.
